ownerIntake.businessType: Mid/large commercial staffing firm operating a national branch network. Two reportable streams: (1) temporary/contract staffing (~80% of revenue), where the firm earns the spread between client bill rate and worker pay rate; (2) permanent / direct-hire placement (~20% of revenue), a fee-based, demand-leading service. Revenue concentrated in light-industrial, logistics, clerical, and administrative verticals. Internal headcount is mostly recruiters and branch staff carried as a largely fixed cost.
ownerIntake.stage: FY2025: Revenue $1,500M (+5.0% YoY vs $1,429M FY2024, decelerating sharply from +12% the prior year). Mix: temp/contract $1,200M (~80%), perm/direct-hire $300M (~20%). Permanent placement revenue DOWN -8% YoY. Gross margin (blended bill-pay spread plus perm fees) 19.5%, down from 21.0% prior year. SG&A ~13.5% of revenue (recruiters, branches), roughly fixed and grew with the prior expansion. EBITDA $90M (6.0% margin) vs $114.3M (8.0%) prior year, a 200 bps decline. Internal staff headcount +4% YoY (added ahead of demand). Client orders -6% YoY; temp hours per week trending -2% sequentially in recent quarters.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Decide before the next quarter (~90 days) whether to freeze internal hiring and right-size the branch/recruiter footprint ahead of a possible demand downturn, or to hold capacity to capture a rebound. Protect EBITDA margin and return to profitable growth without either (a) being caught with excess fixed capacity into a softening cycle or (b) gutting the recruiter base needed to capture a recovery.
ownerConstraints: Bill-rate constraint: bill rates are capped by client budgets and intense competition for orders; clients are resisting the bill-rate increases needed to fully pass through wage inflation, so the firm cannot simply re-price the temp book at will.

Capacity / rebound constraint: recruiter and branch capacity cannot be cut too fast — recruiter tenure and client relationships take 6-12 months to rebuild, so over-cutting destroys the ability to capture a demand rebound.
Cost-input constraint: worker wage inflation is running ~6% and is largely outside the firm's control; pay rates must stay competitive to fill orders, which compresses the spread when bill rates lag.
Fixed-commitment constraint: branch lease commitments are multi-year; the firm cannot instantly shed branch occupancy cost even where order volume has fallen.

Client-concentration constraint: a meaningful share of temp hours sits with a small number of large light-industrial/logistics clients whose order volumes are the most economically sensitive, so demand softening is concentrated and lumpy.
Workforce constraint: temp workers are contingent and re-deployable, but losing skilled recruiters during a freeze risks permanent loss of fill capability in key verticals.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: EBITDA margin fell 200 bps in one year (8.0% to 6.0%) while revenue still grew 5%. Leadership cannot tell how much of the decline is a controllable spread/pricing problem versus a softening demand cycle that the cost base has not adjusted to. Permanent placement (the leading indicator) is already down -8%, client orders are down -6%, and internal staff grew +4% — yet the firm keeps adding capacity against a forecast that may be rolling over. The CEO must commit a capacity decision within 90 days and a wrong call in either direction is costly.

businessProblem: A $1.5B commercial staffing firm has seen EBITDA margin fall from 8.0% to 6.0% (200 bps) in a single year even as reported revenue still grew +5%. Growth has decelerated sharply (from +12% to +5%), and the leading indicators of the staffing cycle are turning negative: permanent / direct-hire placement revenue (the canary for hiring demand) is down -8% YoY, client orders are down -6% YoY, and temp hours per week are trending -2% sequentially. At the same time, the firm has continued to add fixed capacity — internal recruiter/branch headcount grew +4% — and SG&A (~13.5% of revenue) remains largely fixed and was sized during the prior high-growth expansion. Gross spread also compressed 150 bps (21.0% to 19.5%) because worker wage inflation (+6%) outran the bill-rate increases the firm could push through to budget- and competition-constrained clients (+3.5%), leaving ~250 bps of unrecovered wage inflation on the temp book. The core challenge: is the 200 bps EBITDA decline primarily a controllable pricing/spread problem, a structural unit-economics breakdown, or a softening demand cycle that the cost base has been sized ahead of rather than adjusted to? The CEO must decide within ~90 days whether to freeze internal hiring and right-size branches ahead of a possible downturn, or hold capacity for a rebound — and a wrong call in either direction is materially costly.

evidence.finding: EBITDA declined from $114.3M (8.0% margin) FY2024 to $90M (6.0% margin) FY2025 — a 200 bps margin contraction — even though revenue grew +5.0% to $1,500M. Revenue growth itself decelerated sharply from +12% the prior year to +5%, indicating that top-line momentum is rolling over while the cost base has not adjusted.
evidence.source: SEC EDGAR 10-K filings (FY2024, FY2025) and quarterly operating updates

evidence.finding: Permanent / direct-hire placement revenue — the leading indicator of hiring demand in staffing — fell -8% YoY to $300M, and client orders / job openings are down -6% YoY, with temp hours per week trending -2% sequentially over recent quarters. Permanent placement is discretionary and contracts first when clients pull back hiring, so a -8% perm decline alongside -6% orders signals an early-cycle demand contraction, not a one-off.
